title: Exec readout (draft): FP8/INT8 kernel benchmarking sprint (Runtime 1.22.0)
content:
Slide 1 — Title
FP8/INT8 kernel benchmarking sprint: results + rollout plan (Runtime 1.22.0)
Owners: Hiro Tanaka (Kernel), Sofia Ivanova (Scheduling), Jonas Weber (Evals)
PM: Talia Benson


Slide 2 — Executive summary (what changed / why it matters)
- Goal: produce defensible, reproducible FP8/INT8 performance matrix and ship runtime decisions (kernel auto-select + scheduler knobs + canary gates)
- Status: benchmark matrix v1 complete for H100 + A100 across top hosted models; partial coverage on cost SKU (L4) pending capacity + kernel maturity
- Outcome: FP8/INT8 kernels are a net win on throughput and decode cost for most shapes, but end-to-end benefits depend on scheduler + workload mix
- Shipped behind flags with model/region gating + auto rollback (perf canary)


Slide 3 — Headline wins (H100/A100; end-to-end, serving-level)
Notes: numbers below are directional ranges from matrix v1; see Drive: fp8-int8-benchmark-matrix-v1 for per-model breakdown.
- H100 (hosted fleet, mixed prefill/decode):
  - Throughput (tokens/sec): +15% to +30% on top traffic models under realistic concurrency
  - p50 TPOT: -8% to -18% (faster decode)
  - p95 TPOT: -5% to -15% (variance improved after clock pinning + debug logging fix)
  - TTFT: mixed; typically flat to -8%, but a subset saw +3% to +10% regression until scheduler tuning / kernel dispatch tweaks
- A100:
  - Throughput: +8% to +20% (INT8 tends to dominate; FP8 wins are narrower and shape-dependent)
  - TPOT: -5% to -12%
  - TTFT: mostly flat; a few prompt sets sensitive to launch overhead
- Unit-cost proxy (GPU-ms / 1k tokens): -8% to -22% in best regimes; realized savings highest when batching window tuned for mixed workloads


Slide 4 — What we shipped (Runtime 1.22.0 scope)
- Kernel integration + dispatch:
  - FP8 attention kernels behind flag; registry entries + shape guardrails
  - INT8 matmul dispatch rules + fallback behavior for unsupported shapes
  - Kernel auto-selection heuristics by GPU arch + shape regime (see ADR-019)
- Harness + measurement stability:
  - Standardized warmup/measurement loops; artifact metadata export (git SHA, driver/CUDA, clocks, model hash)
  - Runner supports optional GPU clock locking; improved reproducibility across clusters
- Scheduler + instrumentation:
  - Prefill/decode breakdown metrics; queue depth histograms; backpressure counters
  - Default knob adjustments validated for mixed workloads (batching window + backpressure)
- Rollout safety:
  - Perf canary gate per model + region cohort; automatic rollback triggers
  - Metrics tagged by model/GPU/kernel-mode to localize regressions quickly


Slide 5 — Coverage: GPUs, models, workloads
GPUs in matrix v1:
- H100 (primary) — complete
- A100 (primary) — complete
- L4 (cost SKU) — partial (microbench complete; serving-level matrix blocked on capacity + a few missing optimized paths)

Models (top hosted traffic cohort for this sprint):
- Llama-3-class 70B (dense)
- Mixtral-class 8x7B / MoE
- Qwen2.5-class 72B
- Llama-3-class 8B (high-volume latency-sensitive)
- Mistral-class 7B
- Embedding/rerank models (limited focus; only sanity runs)

Workloads:
- Prefill-heavy (long prompts, short generation)
- Decode-heavy (short prompts, long generation)
- Mixed (production-like distribution; concurrency sweep)
- Tool-calling / structured-output variant (limited; used to validate that scheduler interactions don’t invert wins)


Slide 6 — Key finding #1: kernel wins are real, but scheduler determines realized end-to-end gains
- Microbench results show consistent FP8/INT8 kernel wins on compute-bound shapes
- Serving-level results show “winner flips” based on:
  - Prefill/decode interleaving and batching behavior
  - Queue depth/backpressure settings (can reduce kernel utilization if too conservative)
  - Launch overhead sensitivity at low batch / low concurrency (TTFT risk)
- Practical takeaway:
  - Kernel auto-select must be coupled with scheduler profile defaults for each workload regime
  - We should treat “kernel mode” as a joint kernel+scheduler profile, not a single switch


Slide 7 — Key finding #2: shape guardrails + fallbacks are non-negotiable
- INT8 correctness failure reproduced on a small set of shapes (alignment/hidden-dim constraints)
  - Mitigation: strict shape guardrails + automatic fallback to baseline kernels
- FP8 decode perf cliff discovered for KV cache alignment edge case
  - Mitigation: bugfix + hotfix disable FP8 for one problematic regime; track for re-enable
- Practical takeaway:
  - Dispatch logic must be conservative by default; “fast path” only when constraints validated
  - Canary must be model+shape aware (or at least model+workload proxy aware)


Slide 8 — Quality & evals (Applied ML / Evals summary)
- Goal: ensure no unacceptable quality regressions when enabling FP8/INT8 by default
- Status:
  - Quality sanity suite shows no broad regression on most prompt sets
  - One long-context regression identified under FP8 for a specific model family; mitigation is gating FP8 for long-context + requiring eval sign-off for default enablement
- Policy proposal (draft; see Drive: quality-vs-quantization-evals-summary):
  - FP8 default enablement requires: passing sanity suite + “long-context slice” checks for models that receive >X% long-context traffic
  - INT8 default enablement requires: calibration sign-off per model family + a small targeted eval set for summarization + extraction
  - If quality delta exceeds threshold: remain opt-in (flag) and/or fall back to baseline on affected routes


Slide 9 — Reproducibility & benchmarking hygiene (what we fixed)
- Main sources of noise encountered:
  - Driver/CUDA mismatch across clusters
  - GPU clock drift / thermal throttling / shared-node contention
  - Debug logging path perturbing timing measurements
- Mitigations shipped:
  - Runner pins container + driver/CUDA where possible; artifacts record exact versions
  - Optional clock locking for benchmark nodes; warmup rules standardized
  - Removed/gated debug logging; improved artifact uploader metadata
- Remaining gap:
  - Need a dedicated “benchmark lane” with consistent fleet configuration (or stricter scheduling isolation) to reduce re-run cost


Slide 10 — Canary outcome (what happened in practice)
- Canary configuration:
  - Enabled per model + region cohort; thresholds on TTFT, TPOT, tokens/sec, error rate
  - Noise suppression for small samples; tagging improvements for drill-down
- Incident learnings:
  - Canary detected TTFT spike in one EU region and auto-rolled back within minutes
  - Root cause suspected: scheduler + FP8 attention path interacting with low-batch traffic + higher launch overhead
  - Resolution: keep FP8 attention opt-in for affected cohort; require scheduler profile update before re-enable
- Takeaway:
  - Rollout controls worked as intended (detection + rollback), but we need better “low-traffic canary methodology” to reduce false positives while still catching real regressions


Slide 11 — Risks / open issues (next 2–4 weeks)
- Quality risk:
  - FP8 long-context regression for model family X (tracking: keep gated; require eval sign-off)
- Performance risk:
  - TTFT regressions at low batch / low concurrency regimes; needs focused kernel launch overhead work and/or scheduler small-batch policy
- Operational risk:
  - Fleet heterogeneity (driver/CUDA, MIG/partitioning differences) can invalidate comparisons
- Product / comms risk:
  - External performance claims must be footnoted with workload definitions + environment; align with Product (perf transparency)


Slide 12 — Rollout plan (proposed)
Phase 0 (now):
- Keep FP8/INT8 behind flags; run perf canary on 1–2 regions per model
- Default enablement only where: quality sign-off complete + stable TTFT/TPOT over >=N days

Phase 1 (1–2 weeks):
- Expand canary cohorts (additional regions + larger traffic slices)
- Enable INT8 by default for “safe” dense models on H100/A100 where guardrails cover >99% of shapes

Phase 2 (2–4 weeks):
- Re-enable FP8 attention where TTFT regressions addressed (kernel + scheduler profile)
- Add L4 end-to-end matrix and decide default policy for cost SKU (likely INT8-first)

Rollback triggers (already implemented):
- TTFT p95 regression > threshold for >30 min (with min sample)
- TPOT p95 regression > threshold for >30 min
- Error rate increase beyond baseline


Slide 13 — Recommended next investments (what moves the needle most)
1) Scheduling (highest ROI for realized end-to-end gains)
- Build explicit scheduler profiles per workload regime (prefill-heavy vs decode-heavy vs mixed)
- Improve small-batch behavior (TTFT sensitivity) without sacrificing throughput
- Add “shape regime” awareness where feasible (or proxy via prompt/gen length bins)

2) Kernel work (targeted)
- Reduce launch overhead / improve fusion for attention paths in low-batch regimes
- Expand FP8 coverage safely (more shapes, better guardrails) and re-test long-context accuracy
- Improve L4-appropriate kernels (INT8 focus)

3) Fleet / infra (enabling)
- Standardized benchmark lane + pinned driver/CUDA images across benchmark clusters
- Faster allocation of cost SKU capacity for L4 matrix to avoid blind spots in product recommendations


Slide 14 — Decision asks (leadership)
- Approve:
  - Dedicated benchmark lane (capacity + infra effort) to reduce variance and re-run cost
  - Continued work to package “kernel mode + scheduler profile” as a single supported configuration per model/SKU
- Align on:
  - Default enablement policy: INT8-first for A100/L4; FP8 selectively on H100 pending long-context sign-off
  - What performance claims we can publish internally/externally and required footnotes


Slide 15 — Appendix: where to find details
- Benchmark matrix v1 (per model/GPU/workload, aggregates + raw runs): Drive → fp8-int8-benchmark-matrix-v1
- Microbench kernel breakdowns (shapes, launch configs): Drive → kernel-microbench-results-h100-a100
- Evals summary + sign-off criteria draft: Drive → quality-vs-quantization-evals-summary
- Heuristics decision record: Confluence → ADR-019
- Canary runbook + thresholds: perf-canary PRs + Confluence runbook (linked from ENG-7431)


Speaker notes (draft, for Talia/Hiro)
- Be explicit that “wins” are workload-defined; we should not generalize to all prompts/models/SKUs without footnotes.
- Emphasize that canary/rollback worked and reduced customer impact; the remaining ask is to harden defaults and broaden coverage (esp. L4).
- Reinforce that the next 10–20% end-to-end improvement likely comes from scheduler profiles and fleet consistency, not just better kernels.
